candidates.name: Cohere Transcribe Arabic (07-2026)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Built for MSA plus dialects and Arabic-English code-switching. In the vendor's own dialect table it scores 19.16 WER on Egyptian, against 21.38 for OmniASR-LLM-7B, 24.64 for Cohere Transcribe (multilingual) and 28.25 for Whisper-large-v3. The test data is described only as 'various open-source and internal benchmarks'.
candidates.code_switching: Vendor-reported code-switched (AR-EN) WER is 27.84, against 35.37 for OmniASR-7B, 40.95 for Cohere Transcribe and 36.90 for Whisper-v3. The blog says human evaluators found 'English terms were correctly transcribed in Latin script'. The model card warns that code-switching output has some inconsistencies and assumes one language is primary. A language tag is required (ar or en).
candidates.license: Apache-2.0. The weights are gated behind a contact-info form.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: 2B parameters, a Conformer encoder with a Transformer decoder. The model card says CPU works via Transformers (>=5.4). Community GGUF from cstr runs in the CrispASR C++ runtime ('--backend cohere-ar'): Q4_K 1.5 GB (plus an imatrix variant calibrated on Common Voice Arabic), Q8_0 2.4 GB, F16 4.1 GB. Other conversions exist: ONNX (Masterx, abdelmoez98), int8/int4 (NAMAA-Space) and MLX. The cstr card for the parent 03-2026 model reports RTFx of about 1.03-1.08 with 8 CPU threads on an 11 s clip (CPU not named). Expect roughly real time or slower on an i5-1245U (unverified). The small Q4_K download is manageable at 1.5 MB/s. It has no timestamps and no diarization, and the model card notes it is 'eager to transcribe, even non-speech sounds', so VAD chunking is advisable.
candidates.diarization: None, and no timestamps (model card and Cohere docs). Pair it with separate diarization.
candidates.reported_accuracy: Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard average is 25.87 WER / 11.80 CER, the best open model per the vendor. Per set: SADA 37.47, CV 5.82, MASC-clean 19.60 (the card; the blog table shows 15.54), MASC-noisy 27.07, MGB-2 15.54, Casablanca 49.71. All vendor-reported.
candidates.cost_and_free_tier: The weights are free. The hosted Cohere API has model name 'cohere-transcribe-arabic-07-2026', which docs say is free for experimentation on a trial key: 5 req/min for audio transcriptions, 1,000 API calls a month overall, files up to 25 MB (FLAC/MP3/OGG/WAV). A language parameter is required. Trial keys may not be used for production or commercial work.
candidates.notes: Released 2026-07-07. This is the strongest general open Arabic model released in 2026 on published numbers, and the only one with a vendor-reported code-switching score. The 8 kHz input is auto-resampled to 16 kHz. Community tool AliOsm/cohere-transcribe adds Silero VAD and MMS forced-alignment word timestamps, but it states that full-model CPU inference was not validated. For the free hosted path: an 80-min 8 kHz 16-bit WAV is about 77 MB, so it must be split or compressed below 25 MB. Because the API returns no timestamps, the practical recipe is to diarize locally first and send merged speaker turns as separate requests, which uses up the 1,000 calls a month quickly. The QwenCleo authors did not include this model in their Egyptian table; they only tested the 03-2026 multilingual parent.

candidates.name: QwenCleo-ASR (Egyptian and code-switch fine-tune of Qwen3-ASR-1.7B)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Fine-tuned specifically for Egyptian Arabic and Arabic-English code-switching on 'hundreds of hours of Egyptian podcast speech'.
candidates.code_switching: The card says embedded English stays in Latin script (examples: 'YouTube', 'already', 'Microsoft Excel'). This directly targets the transliteration problem the user measured on base Qwen3-ASR.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Same architecture as Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, about 2B params in BF16. No GGUF is published and CPU use is not documented. ggml-org's Qwen3-ASR GGUFs were made with llama.cpp convert_hf_to_gguf.py, so converting this fine-tune the same way should give a drop-in replacement for the user's existing Q8 llama.cpp setup, at roughly 2.2 GB for Q8_0 and about 0.7x real time like the base. Both points are unverified: conversion of this repo was not tested.
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: Self-reported on the authors' own Egyptian plus code-switching test set (3,699 utterances, 'Egyptian-aware normalization'): QwenCleo 19.85 WER / 10.52 CER, with code-switched utterances at 20.75 WER. Same test set: Arabic-Whisper-CodeSwitching 37.98, NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 (0.6B) 38.04, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B base 41.51, Whisper-large-v3-turbo fine-tune 50.83, Cohere Transcribe 03-2026 53.20, MasriSwitch-Gemma3n 57.30, Whisper-large-v3 63.94, Whisper-large-v3-turbo 73.83. The base result is close to the user's own ArzEn measurement for Qwen3-ASR (43% WER).
candidates.notes: Updated June 2026, about 3.4k downloads. All accuracy figures are self-reported by the fine-tuner on their own test set. The model card is official for this model, but the claims have not been independently verified. It is the most direct fix for the user's 'English transliterated into Arabic letters' problem and slots into the llama.cpp pipeline they already run. Worth a local A/B on the user's 40 ArzEn clips.

candidates.name: Audar-ASR-V1-Flash
candidates.egyptian_arabic: The card claims coverage of MSA plus Gulf, Egyptian, Levantine and Maghrebi dialects, English, and 28 other languages. It gives no Egyptian-only number.
candidates.code_switching: Code-switched Arabic-English is claimed. Latin-script behaviour is not documented.
candidates.license: AudarAI Open License v1.0. Per the card it allows commercial use, redistribution and fine-tuning, with attribution and the license included.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: 0.78B params (0.60B decoder and 0.19B audio encoder). Official GGUF runs with llama.cpp llama-mtmd-cli: Q4_K_M decoder about 0.40 GB or Q8_0 about 0.64 GB, plus a BF16 audio projector of about 0.38 GB. That is a tiny download and should be faster than Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on CPU (estimate). The context window is 30 s, so VAD chunking is required, and the card warns long recordings may drift.
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard average is 32.04 WER. Per set: SADA 44.36, CV-18 15.38, MASC-clean 22.56, MASC-noisy 34.19, MGB-2 17.05, Casablanca 58.71. Self-reported.
candidates.notes: The output prefix format ('language Arabic<asr_text>') and the parameter split match Qwen3-ASR-0.6B, so it is probably a Qwen3-ASR-0.6B derivative (my inference, unverified). The release date is not stated (2026). It is a very low-cost CPU trial because it uses the same llama.cpp mtmd path the user already has.

candidates.name: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 ASR Streaming 0.6B (multilingual, 40 locales)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Arabic is supported as the single locale 'ar-AR' (no dialect locales). The QwenCleo authors' third-party Egyptian plus code-switch test puts it 3rd of 13 at 38.04 WER / 19.72 CER, ahead of base Qwen3-ASR-1.7B (41.51) and far ahead of Whisper-large-v3 (63.94).
candidates.code_switching: Not documented. On the same third-party test, code-switched utterances scored 41.44 WER / 25.66 CER, worse than Arabic-only (36.23). Whether English is kept in Latin script is unverified.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: 600M-param cache-aware FastConformer-RNNT with language-ID prompt conditioning. An official Q8_0 GGUF (742 MB) sits in the NVIDIA repo. Community GGUF from cstr: Q4_K 458 MB, Q8_0 686 MB, F16 1.3 GB. It runs on CPU via NVIDIA's NeMo-Speech.cpp (ggml; CPU/Vulkan/Metal/CUDA backends; offline WAV and batch directory modes; ASR can be combined with Sortformer or Nemotron 3 diarization) and via CrispASR ('--backend nemotron --language ar-AR'). Speed on a laptop CPU is not published. FastConformer-class models are among the fastest on CPU, and CrispASR cites parakeet 0.6B at about 2.9x real time, so this is likely much faster than real time on the i5 (estimate).
candidates.diarization: Not in the ASR model. NeMo-Speech.cpp bundles Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2 and Nemotron 3 Diarization for combined runs.
candidates.reported_accuracy: Official FLEURS Arabic WER: 12.03 (1.12 s chunk, LangID), 13.17 at an 80 ms chunk. Third-party Egyptian plus code-switch: 38.04 WER (self-reported by the QwenCleo authors).
candidates.notes: Released 2026-06-04. It has built-in punctuation and capitalization. This is the best speed-to-quality CPU option among the general models, and it comes with an official NVIDIA C++ runtime that also does diarization. Sample-rate handling for 8 kHz is not documented; NeMo-Speech.cpp says it handles common WAV sample rates automatically.

candidates.name: Meta Omnilingual ASR (omniASR CTC / LLM / LLM-Unlimited v2)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Egyptian Arabic is explicitly supported as 'arz_Arab'. I confirmed it in the repo's lang_ids.py, along with arb, apc, ary, aeb, acm, ars, apd and other Arabic varieties. Third-party arz test WER (Arab Voices paper): LLM-7B-v2 34.8 (best of 14 models), LLM-300M-v2 41.7, LLM-1B-v2 49.38, LLM-3B-v2 48.76, CTC-300M-v2 58.87, CTC-1B-v2 45.7, CTC-3B-v2 42.28, CTC-7B-v2 45.59.
candidates.code_switching: Not evaluated officially. Cohere's evaluation puts OmniASR-LLM-7B at 35.37 WER on code-switched AR-EN. Latin-script handling is unverified. Language conditioning to a single code (arz_Arab) may push English toward Arabic script (unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Official downloads are fp32 .pt files: CTC 300M 1.3 GiB, CTC 1B 3.7 GiB, LLM-300M 6.1 GiB (1.63B params incl. LLM), LLM-1B 8.5 GiB, LLM-3B 17 GiB, LLM-7B 30 GiB. Official benchmarks are on A100 only, and CPU is not documented. sherpa-onnx ports exist for CTC 300M and 1B (int8 and fp32; 300M int8 is 348 MB, RTF 0.225 on the doc's test CPU). CrispASR also lists OmniASR CTC and LLM backends. CTC and standard LLM models only accept audio under 40 s, so VAD chunking is needed; the LLM-Unlimited v2 variants handle any length. The 7B is not feasible on this laptop. CTC-1B int8 via sherpa-onnx is the practical CPU choice, though its arz accuracy is weaker (45.7).
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: Arabic leaderboard average for OmniASR-LLM-7B is 28.32 WER, the previous best open model per Cohere. Per set: SADA 41.61, CV 9.75, MASC-clean 19.69, MASC-noisy 29.29, MGB-2 14.13, Casablanca 56.46. Cohere's Egyptian subset: 21.38. Arab Voices arz numbers are listed above.
candidates.notes: Released November 2025; v2 and Unlimited variants followed later. The smallest LLM variant (LLM-300M-v2, 6.1 GiB fp32) does surprisingly well on arz (41.7), but it has no official quantized or CPU path and the download is heavy at 1.5 MB/s (about 70 min). The per-language CER CSV linked from the README returned 404 when I fetched it.

candidates.name: OpenAI Whisper large-v3 / large-v3-turbo
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Arabic is among its 99 languages. Third-party arz test WER (Arab Voices): large-v3 35.69, which is second best, just behind OmniASR-LLM-7B (34.8); large-v3-turbo 48.16. Cohere's Egyptian subset: large-v3 28.25.
candidates.code_switching: Cohere's code-switched AR-EN WER is 36.90 for large-v3. On the QwenCleo Egyptian plus CS set: large-v3 63.94, turbo 73.83. A secondary source describes Whisper transliterating English terms (e.g. 'ديبلوي' for deploy) or translating whole sentences. A technique to counter this is the prompt-seeding entry below.
candidates.license: HF model card lists Apache-2.0 for large-v3 and MIT for turbo.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: large-v3 has 1.55B params. Turbo has 809M, keeping 4 decoder layers instead of 32, which gives 'minor quality degradation'. faster-whisper (CTranslate2) int8 on CPU with Silero VAD and a batched pipeline is what the user already measured at about 1.6-2x real time for large-v3. Turbo is several times faster but clearly worse on Egyptian.
candidates.diarization: None (use WhisperX or pyannote, or the user's WeSpeaker pipeline).
candidates.reported_accuracy: Arabic leaderboard average for large-v3 is 36.86 WER (paper and Cohere blog). Dolphin paper: FLEURS-ar 10.5, CV17-ar 33.5.
candidates.notes: No newer open-weight OpenAI ASR model was found. OpenAI's newer transcribers (gpt-4o-transcribe and mini) are API-only. Note the conflict: the user found large-v3 best by ear, the Arab Voices numbers support that, but the QwenCleo code-switch benchmark ranks it poorly. That table is likely sensitive to script and normalization, since Latin versus Arabic spelling of English words is penalized.

candidates.name: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B / 0.6B (base)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: 'Arabic' is one of 30 languages; the card mentions no Arabic dialects. The user already measured it on ArzEn: 43% WER, 16% English kept in Latin script. On the QwenCleo Egyptian plus CS test, 1.7B scores 41.51 WER.
candidates.code_switching: Not documented. The tech report only mentions cross-lingual support for the ForcedAligner. The user observed English transliterated into Arabic script.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: ggml-org GGUFs: 1.7B Q8_0 2.17 GB, 0.6B Q8_0 805 MB. Runs in llama.cpp (the user's setup), CrispASR and a Rust/candle engine. The tech report says a single input can be at most 20 minutes, so chunk the 80-min calls.
candidates.diarization: None. Qwen3-ForcedAligner-0.6B gives timestamps for clips up to 5 min, in 11 languages.
candidates.reported_accuracy: FLEURS-ar: 1.7B 16.98 WER, 0.6B 25.51 (tech report, Table A.2b).
candidates.notes: Released 2026-01-29; native Transformers support added 2026-06-26. Its main value here is as the base for the Egyptian fine-tunes QwenCleo-ASR and (probably) Audar-ASR-V1-Flash. No Qwen3.5-ASR open release was found.

candidates.name: Microsoft VibeVoice-ASR (7B) with GGUF / CrispASR port
candidates.egyptian_arabic: 'Arabic' is in the model card's list of 51 languages, but the tech report has no Arabic results. The report admits 'multilingual forgetting' because SFT focused on English, Chinese and code-switching. Egyptian quality is unknown.
candidates.code_switching: Claims to 'natively handle code-switching within and across utterances', with no language setting needed. It is untested on Arabic-English.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: About 9B params in total (a Qwen2.5-7B decoder plus acoustic and semantic tokenizers at 7.5 Hz). Official inference needs an NVIDIA GPU. Community CrispASR C++ port with GGUF: Q4_K about 4.5-5 GB, Q8_0 9.45 GB, F16 16 GB. The author says Q4_K 'runs comfortably on a 16 GB box'. Input must be 24 kHz mono (upsample from 8 kHz). No CPU speed figures are published. With only 6-8 GB free RAM and a 7B decoder, expect slower than real time on the i5-1245U (estimate). A 5 GB download takes about an hour at 1.5 MB/s.
candidates.diarization: Yes, built in. A single pass over up to 60 min of audio (64K tokens) outputs speaker ID, start/end timestamps and text as JSON. The CrispASR port says diarization, timestamps and hotwords are wired in.
candidates.reported_accuracy: No Arabic numbers. English Open ASR Leaderboard average is 7.77 WER. MLC-Challenge: DER 4.28, cpWER 11.48, tcpWER 13.02 (11 languages, no Arabic).
candidates.notes: It is the only general open model that does ASR, diarization and timestamps together over a whole hour of audio, which is attractive for 2-speaker calls. The 80-min calls exceed its 60-min window and need splitting. Worth a spot check only if RAM allows. The official CPU variant VibeVoice-ASR-BitNet (VibeASR.cpp, 1.58 GB, RTF about 0.33-0.37 on an i7-13700 with 4-8 threads) lists only 7 languages and not Arabic, and its docs do not mention diarization.

candidates.name: Microsoft VibeVoice-ASR-BitNet + VibeASR.cpp
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Arabic is not listed. The card lists English, Chinese, French, Italian, Korean, Portuguese and Vietnamese ('7 languages').
candidates.code_switching: Not documented
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Built for CPU: the LM is swapped to Qwen2.5-1.5B with I2_S/I8_S quantization, 1.58 GB total, AVX2+FMA. RTF on an Intel i7-13700 is 0.37 with 4 threads and 0.33 with 8.
candidates.diarization: Not mentioned in its docs
candidates.reported_accuracy: LibriSpeech-clean 2.41, FLEURS-en 5.21. No Arabic.
candidates.notes: Listed for completeness. It is probably not usable for Egyptian Arabic, since Arabic is absent from its supported languages.

candidates.name: Mistral Voxtral (Mini 4B Realtime 2602 open weights; Mini/Small 2507; Transcribe V2 API)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Voxtral Realtime 4B (Feb 2026) supports 13 languages including Arabic, with FLEURS-ar WER 22.53 at 480 ms delay. That is worse than Qwen3-ASR-1.7B (16.98) or Nemotron 3.5 (12.03). Voxtral Mini 3B 2507 has no Arabic among its 8 languages. The third-party arz test gives Voxtral-Small-24B-2507 43.25 WER.
candidates.code_switching: Not documented
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Realtime 4B is about 3.4B LM plus a 970M encoder. The official recommendation is a GPU with 16 GB or more. antirez/voxtral.c is a pure-C CPU implementation, and there are also MLX and Rust ports. It is heavy for an i5-U laptop; on an M3 Max it runs about 2.5x faster than real time. Small 24B is not feasible.
candidates.diarization: The open Realtime model has none documented. The API model Voxtral Mini Transcribe V2 (not open) has diarization, word timestamps, context biasing, Arabic, and audio up to 3 hours per request.
candidates.reported_accuracy: FLEURS-ar 22.53 (Realtime, official). arz 43.25 (Small 24B, Arab Voices paper).
candidates.cost_and_free_tier: API: Transcribe V2 costs $0.003/min, Realtime $0.006/min. I did not confirm a free tier on the official page.
candidates.notes: Among Mistral's options, the hosted Transcribe V2 is the most relevant: it has Arabic plus diarization. The open 4B model is not a strong Arabic candidate for CPU.

candidates.name: Google Gemma 4 (E2B / E4B / 12B audio) and Gemma 3n
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Described as trained for multilingual ASR, and Gemma 3n on 'over 140 spoken languages'. No per-language or Arabic ASR numbers are published. A dev.to post reports that Arabic works and that E4B is much better than E2B (secondary). The Egyptian fine-tune MasriSwitch-Gemma3n (E4B) scored 57.30 WER on the QwenCleo Egyptian plus CS set.
candidates.code_switching: Not documented
candidates.license: Gemma 4 is Apache-2.0 per its model card. Gemma 3n uses the Gemma Terms of Use.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: E2B has 2.3B effective params (5.1B total), E4B 4.5B effective, the 12B about 12B. Audio is capped at 30 s per clip for Gemma 4, so chunking is needed. llama.cpp added the Gemma 4 audio conformer (PR #21421; BF16 mmproj recommended; llama-mtmd-cli --audio), with reported mmproj and server rough edges. It is heavy for the laptop and unproven on Arabic.
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: No Arabic ASR figures published
candidates.notes: Low priority. There is no Arabic evidence from Google, and the only Egyptian datapoint, from a fine-tune, is weak.

candidates.name: Meta SeamlessM4T v2 Large
candidates.egyptian_arabic: 'arz' (Egyptian Arabic) is listed as a supported speech source language. Third-party arz test WER is 37.61, third best of 14 models, behind OmniASR-LLM-7B and Whisper-large-v3.
candidates.code_switching: Not documented. As a translation-oriented model it may normalize to one script (unverified).
candidates.license: CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial; acceptable for a personal trial)
candidates.cpu_feasibility: 2.3B params in Transformers. It runs on CPU but slowly, with no official quantized or GGUF port. Long-form audio needs chunking.
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: arz 37.61 WER (Arab Voices paper, third-party)
candidates.notes: It is decent on Egyptian but older, has an NC license and no CPU tooling. Not a top pick.

candidates.name: Meta MMS-1B-all
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Poor: third-party arz test WER is 74.32, the worst of the 14 models in the Arab Voices paper.
candidates.code_switching: Not supported in any meaningful way
candidates.license: CC-BY-NC-4.0 (per Meta's MMS release; not re-checked in this sweep)
candidates.cpu_feasibility: 1B-param CTC with adapters. Runs on CPU.
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: arz 74.32 WER (third-party)
candidates.notes: Superseded by Omnilingual ASR. Not recommended.

candidates.name: Dolphin (DataoceanAI) base / small
candidates.egyptian_arabic: It has an explicit Egyptian region token 'ar-EG', plus ar-SA, ar-AE, ar-LVT, ar-MA and others. Arabic results in the paper: small scores FLEURS 14.2, CV17 40.1 and Dataocean 18.7, against Whisper-large-v3 at 10.5, 33.5 and 21.7.
candidates.code_switching: Not documented
candidates.cpu_feasibility: base 0.1B and small 0.4B are released; medium 0.9B and large 1.7B are not public. Small models of this size should be CPU-friendly. CrispASR lists a Dolphin backend.
candidates.diarization: None (the model has VAD, segmentation and LID)
candidates.reported_accuracy: As above, from the Dolphin paper (self-reported)
candidates.notes: A small, fast option with an Egyptian dialect tag, but its Arabic accuracy is below Whisper-large-v3 on public sets. It is a cheap sanity test at best.

candidates.name: Moonshine Tiny Arabic (Flavors of Moonshine)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: An Arabic monolingual 27M-param model; dialect coverage is not specified.
candidates.code_switching: The card says it transcribes 'Arabic speech audio into Arabic text (with code-switching)'. Metrics are not given, and the script of the English output is unknown.
candidates.license: 'other' per the HF card; terms not verified
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Tiny (27M), with an ONNX port. CrispASR reports Moonshine at about 16x real time on CPU.
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: FLEURS-ar 20.76 WER, CV17-ar 36.55 (self-reported)
candidates.notes: The card warns about hallucination and repetition. Too small for serious Egyptian tech calls, but useful as an ultra-fast draft pass.

candidates.name: Fun-ASR-MLT-Nano-2512 (Tongyi / FunAudioLLM)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Arabic is among 31 languages, with the main optimization on East and Southeast Asian languages. There are no Egyptian or dialect claims.
candidates.code_switching: Not documented for Arabic
candidates.cpu_feasibility: 800M params. The Fun-ASR GitHub mentions separate FunASR, vLLM and llama.cpp deployment paths (not verified for this checkpoint). Timestamps and diarization are listed as TODO.
candidates.diarization: Not yet (TODO on the card)
candidates.reported_accuracy: No clear Arabic WER on the card. The fetch summary returned a garbled figure (15.28), which I could not verify.
candidates.notes: Breadth entry. There is no evidence it handles Egyptian or code-switching well.

candidates.name: Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B (and Qwen3.5-Omni)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Arabic is among 19 speech-input languages. Third-party arz test WER is 68.6, which is poor.
candidates.code_switching: Not documented
candidates.license: Apache-2.0 (Qwen3-Omni; not re-checked in this sweep)
candidates.cpu_feasibility: A 30B MoE (3B active), far too large for 6-8 GB of free RAM. Qwen3.5-Omni is described as 'hundreds of billions of parameters', and I found no open weights for it.
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: arz 68.6 WER (Arab Voices paper)
candidates.notes: Not recommended: poor on Egyptian and infeasible on this CPU.

candidates.name: Cohere Transcribe 03-2026 (multilingual parent)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Arabic is among 14 languages. Cohere's Egyptian subset: 24.64 WER. QwenCleo Egyptian plus CS test: 53.20 WER.
candidates.code_switching: Cohere's code-switched AR-EN WER is 40.95. Cohere says it 'successfully transcribes (En, X) code-switched audio, but we didn't explicitly train the model to do this'.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: 2B params. Community GGUF from cstr ranges from Q4_K 1.21 GB to F16 3.85 GB, at RTFx about 1.03-1.08 with 8 CPU threads in CrispASR. ONNX int8 ports exist (vigneshlabs, tristanripke).
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: Arabic leaderboard average 30.67 WER (Cohere blog)
candidates.cost_and_free_tier: Free weights. The hosted trial key is the same as for the Arabic model.
candidates.notes: Use the Arabic 07-2026 variant instead; it is clearly better on Egyptian and on code-switching.

candidates.name: NVIDIA FastConformer Arabic (stt_ar_fastconformer_hybrid_large_pcd_v1.0)
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Trained on about 1,100 h, mostly MSA (MASC, CV, FLEURS, Quran recitation). The card warns it 'can have poor performance in dialectal Arabic speech'. The Egyptian fine-tune NAMAA-Space/EgypTalk-ASR-v2 is built on it.
candidates.code_switching: Not supported (Arabic-only output with diacritics)
candidates.cpu_feasibility: 115M params, very light. A community sherpa-onnx port exists (mah92/sherpa-onnx-nemo-ctc-ar-fastconformer-hybrid-large-pcd-v1.0-non-streaming-2024-12-25).
candidates.diarization: None
candidates.reported_accuracy: MASC 16.67, CV17 25.60, FLEURS 12.94 WER. The 2024-2025 Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard had NVIDIA conformers at the top.

It feeds MohamedRashad-CS-Whisper, IbrahimAmin, mohammedaly22-turbo, MasriSwitch, Seif-Eldeen-Sameh, Metro and possibly QwenCleo. Scores for these models on ArzEn clips may be inflated, so confirm on the user's own tech calls or the Perle set.

gaps: I found no open model with published results on 8 kHz telephone-band Arabic. Every candidate expects 16 kHz input. Only Audar mentions telephone channels in its training data, and it lists 'heavily code-switched telephony' as a weakness. Upsampling 8 kHz audio to 16 kHz may still lose accuracy, so this has to be tested locally.
No candidate reports numbers on long (16-80 min) Egyptian tech meetings. The Qwen3-ASR-family models (Audar, QwenCleo, lemura) use 30 s windows and need external chunking. Cohere chunks internally.

I could not find any Egyptian-specific or ArzEn WER for Cohere Transcribe Arabic or Audar-ASR-V1. Cohere's Egyptian (19.16) and code-switching (27.84) figures come from an unpublished internal test set, and its own card calls code-switching performance 'inconsistent'.
QwenCleo-ASR and Metro-ASR report numbers on an unpublished 3,699-utterance test set. I could not check its sources or whether it overlaps with their training data.

I could not inspect ahmedheakl/arzen-llm-speech-ds (HTTP 401, private or removed). So I cannot confirm whether the ArzEn test utterances ended up inside MohamedRashad/arabic-english-code-switching, which would contaminate the user's 40-clip ArzEn test.

I found no GGUF or CTranslate2 conversion of QwenCleo-ASR, the Seif-Eldeen-Sameh transformers model (only its own CT2 build), ahmedheakl/arazn-whisper-*, or IbrahimAmin's code-switching Whisper-small. I did not confirm that llama.cpp's Qwen3-ASR converter handles these fine-tunes.

I did not confirm that mradermacher's lemura-arabic-asr-qwen3 GGUF and mmproj actually run in llama.cpp's mtmd path; I only inferred it from the file names and the architecture. Audar's GGUF is documented to run.
The MasriSwitch-Gemma3n GGUF repo has no audio encoder or mmproj file, so it appears unusable for audio. This is inferred from the file list and not tested.

I found no open-weight ASR model from SDAIA or HUMAIN (ALLaM is text-only in what I found), KAUST, or QCRI. QCRI's Fanar Aura-STT appears to be platform-only; I did not verify its terms or any weights.
Munsit (CNTXT) is API or on-prem only, with no open weights, and I found no free-tier details.

I found no NVIDIA Parakeet Arabic model. parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 is European-only, and one author reports Arabic transfer failed (WER about 0.93). NVIDIA's Arabic offerings are the FastConformer hybrid models and Nemotron 3.5's ar-AR locale.

I could not find released model weights from the ESCWA code-switching work (QCRI) or the Casablanca paper's own fine-tunes (UBC); the Casablanca text says an earlier group's comparable models were never released.

I did not open the AudarAI Community License text itself; I relied on the card's summary. Check whether personal/MVP use qualifies before relying on Turbo, or use Flash, which is under the Open license.

CPU speed on the user's i5-1245U is estimated from reports on other hardware: transcribe.cpp on a Ryzen 7 4750U, Seif's CT2 on 2 vCPUs, Metro's 'laptop CPU' claim. None of it was measured on this machine.

The FLEURS 'ar_eg' split, which the Cohere GGUF ports and the NVIDIA sherpa export report as 'Egyptian', is read FLORES sentences (mostly MSA text spoken by Egyptian speakers), not spontaneous dialect (FLEURS paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12446). Those numbers overstate performance on real Egyptian conversation.

candidates.egyptian_arabic: The NADI 2025 system scored EGY 20.88 / 7.33, the best result in the shared task, using a 121M Conformer CTC with 15k h weakly labelled pretraining. Munsit markets 25+ dialects including Egyptian.
candidates.notes: The shared-task system is not necessarily the production API. Free tier and code-switching behaviour not verified.

candidates.name: pyannote speaker-diarization-community-1 (diarization evidence on telephone audio)
candidates.diarization:
Model card (benchmark updated 2025-09), CALLHOME (part 2, telephone), DER with no collar and overlap counted:
- community-1: 26.7%
- legacy 3.1: 28.5%
- precision-2 (paid pyannoteAI): 16.6%
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Pipelines run on CPU by default.
candidates.notes: CALLHOME is multilingual 8 kHz two-party telephone speech, the same shape as the user's calls. The ~27% DER includes missed and false-alarm speech, not only speaker confusion. No Arabic-specific DER was found for any system, and ElevenLabs publishes no DER.

candidates.name: Code-switching-aware evaluation (transliteration-normalised WER, BERTScore)
candidates.code_switching: Hamed et al. built a 1,304-utterance human-acceptance corpus on dialectal Arabic/English code-switched speech. The metric that correlates best with human judgement is transliteration followed by text normalisation. Perle shows WER inflates gaps about 3x because it penalises Arabic-script English.
candidates.notes: Implication for the user's own tests: Qwen3-ASR's 43% WER partly reflects transliteration rather than recognition errors. Scoring after transliteration normalisation, or reporting Latin-retention separately as already done, gives a fairer comparison.

gaps: No published WER for ANY commercial API (ElevenLabs, Google, Azure, OpenAI, Speechmatics, Soniox, Deepgram, AssemblyAI) on the standard ArzEn test set; the only Egyptian code-switching commercial comparison is Perle (arXiv 2605.19069), which uses voice-actor headset recordings, not phone calls.

ElevenLabs publishes no official Egyptian-dialect or code-switching WER; its docs place Arabic in a 10–20% WER bucket, while its Arabic marketing page claims FLEURS 3.1% alongside a table showing 11.1%, which is inconsistent.

No study found that measures any Arabic ASR system on 8 kHz versus 16 kHz audio. CALLHOME Egyptian (telephone) is included in the Arab Voices Egyptian pool, but it is resampled to 16 kHz and not broken out per dataset. The Maqsam call-centre benchmark is real telephone audio but uses 2024-era models and 'standardized at 16kHz' audio.
No accuracy evidence found for ElevenLabs Scribe, Speechmatics, Deepgram or Soniox on narrowband telephone Arabic specifically.
Soniox Arabic WER figures (16.2% vs competitors) appear only in search snippets; the soniox.com compare pages returned 404 when fetched, so they are unverified.

Deepgram Nova-3 Arabic (Jan 2026, includes ar-EG) publishes only a chart and a 'up to ~40% lower WER' claim with no numeric Egyptian WER. AssemblyAI Universal-3.5 Pro publishes no Arabic-specific WER.
Speechmatics' Arabic-English code-switching numbers (Melia 1 15.1% mixed error rate; bilingual model 6.3%) are internal self-reports with an undescribed dataset.
Mixat (Emirati-English code-switching) paper tables could not be fetched (HTML 404); only ArTST results on Mixat (21.66 WER) were obtained.
ESCWA-CS: no 2023–2026 results with modern models (Whisper-v3, Qwen3-ASR, commercial APIs) were found.
CS-FLEURS (Interspeech 2025): Arabic-English CER numbers were not retrieved.
Bulbul (arXiv 2608.21950, Aug 2026) and PolySpeech-100 (2606.01016): per-dialect or Egyptian results were not retrievable from the abstracts.
An Islamic University Journal 2026 paper evaluating 4 ASR systems (plus GPT/ALLAM post-correction) on Egyptian, Chami, Hijazi and Najdi speech could not be downloaded, so its numbers are unknown.
'EgyAlex' dataset: not found under that name. Related sets found: MGB-3, CALLHOME Egyptian, ASR-EgArbCSC, MAdel121/arabic-egy-cleaned.
Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR (arXiv 2609.07549, Sept 2026): no Arabic numbers in the abstract; unclear whether Arabic dialects or open weights are included.
QwenCleo-ASR has no published GGUF and its evaluation is single-author, possibly in-domain; it was not validated independently.
Audar-ASR-V1 English-in-Latin-script behaviour and Egyptian-only WER are not published.

No Arabic telephone diarization DER was found for any system, including ElevenLabs Scribe diarization. Google Chirp 3 lists no Arabic locale for diarization, and Azure ar-EG diarization support was not confirmed from the language table.
Model ids for ArTST v2/v3 (MBZUAI) and the Casablanca 'whisper-egyptian' checkpoint were not verified on Hugging Face.

candidates.name: ElevenLabs Scribe v2 (batch speech-to-text)
candidates.license: Proprietary SaaS. The Free plan has no commercial license (fine for a personal trial).
candidates.cost_and_free_tier: Official pages disagree on how much the free plan gives. (a) The API pricing page lists 'Free / Pay as you go' at $0 with Scribe v2 at $0.22/hour and '4 hours 30 minutes' of Scribe v2 included (about $1 of usage; the same column shows 10,000 TTS characters). API usage 'is billed in US dollars, not credits'. (b) The ElevenCreative pricing page says Free = 10,000 credits a month shared across all products, with 'Speech to Text 330 credits per minute' (about 30 min a month). The API STT landing page says 'Sign up for free and get 10,000 credits instantly. No credit card required.' Paid rates: $0.22/h batch, $0.39/h realtime, keyterm prompting +$0.05/h, entity detection +$0.07/h. Starter is $6/month (27 h of Scribe included per the API page). Payment is by card, Apple Pay or Google Pay.
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Arabic (ara) is in Scribe v2's own WER table in the 'Good (>10% to ≤20% WER)' tier (self-reported). ElevenLabs' Arabic STT landing page lists 'Modern Standard Arabic, Egyptian, Levantine..., Gulf, Maghrebi'. Independent evidence: in Perle.ai's benchmark (arXiv 2605.19069, May 2026), Scribe v2 scored 13.1% WER on Egyptian Arabic–English code-switched speech, against 45.9% for the next-best system.
candidates.code_switching: The only official code-switching claim covers Indic–English: 'Scribe v2 transcribes English words in English, regardless of the surrounding language' (April 2026 blog). There is no official Arabic–English claim. The Perle benchmark found it best on Egyptian and Saudi Arabic–English and suggested it 'consistently picks a single script convention', which points to English being kept in Latin script. This last point is third-party inference.
candidates.diarization: diarize=true supports up to 32 speakers. num_speakers and diarization_threshold are adjustable. Word-level timestamps are included.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Hosted, so no local compute. An 80-min 8 kHz 16-bit mono WAV is about 77 MB. Converting to FLAC or Opus first cuts upload time on a slow link. Limits: up to 3 GB per file per the docs (the API reference says <5 GB direct, <2 GB via source_url) and up to 10 hours per file (1 hour in multichannel mode).
candidates.reported_accuracy: Self-reported: Arabic is in the 10–20% WER tier (ElevenLabs language table, benchmark not specified). Third-party: Egyptian Ar–En code-switching WER 13.1%, BERTScore about 0.939; overall mean WER across 4 code-switching pairs 13.2% (Perle.ai, arXiv 2605.19069). Test conditions: 300 utterances per pair, voice actors on headset/USB mics (not 8 kHz phone), diarization off. The authors work at Perle.ai, a data vendor.
candidates.notes: This is the strongest documented candidate for the use case. Data: non-Enterprise data is used 'to improve the quality of our audio models' by default. Anyone can opt out under Profile > Terms and privacy > Data use > 'Improve the models for everyone'. The API has enable_logging=false ('zero retention mode'); whether a Free account may use it is not stated. Free-tier gaps: the size of the free STT allowance (4.5 h vs about 30 min) and an undocumented per-request credit cap on Free ('The limit depends on whether you are on the Free tier or a paid subscription') could block one 80-min file. Keyterm prompting (up to 1000 terms) can bias toward tech vocabulary but costs +$0.05/h.

candidates.name: Speechmatics (Arabic–English bilingual 'ar_en' pack; Melia 1 multilingual; Enhanced/Standard)
candidates.id_or_url: Batch API with transcription_config.language='ar_en' (bilingual pack) or the Melia 1 model. Docs: https://docs.speechmatics.com/speech-to-text/languages
candidates.cost_and_free_tier: Free plan: '$100 in credit, no card required' (pricing page last updated 31 July 2026). Without a card on file, service pauses when credit reaches zero. Batch rates: Melia 1 $0.129/h, Standard $0.24/h, Enhanced $0.40/h. $100 covers about 250 h of Enhanced or about 775 h of Melia 1. Pro is pay-as-you-go (billed per second, 20% off above 500 h/month). An opt-in 'Model Training' programme takes 33% off in exchange for training use of your data.
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Official: 'Global Arabic gives high-accuracy transcription across many accents and dialects, including (but not limited to) Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and Arabic spoken in the Gulf, Egypt, and the Levant.' The Arabic landing page names Gulf, Egyptian and Levantine.

Melia 1 'transcribes multilingual speech in a single transcript, including speakers who switch language mid-conversation', and Arabic is in its Multilingual list (batch only). The docs do not say whether English words come out in Latin or Arabic script.
candidates.diarization: Yes. Batch 'diarization': 'speaker' with speaker_sensitivity (0–1) and prefer_current_speaker. The March 2026 bilingual-model announcement says it 'supports speaker diarization and speaker focus'. No speaker-count limit is documented. Diarization adds 10–50% to processing time.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Hosted. Batch upload must be under 1 GB in the POST body; larger files go via fetch URL. No current max duration was found (legacy docs said 2 h per job). Audio, transcripts and config are stored 7 days.
candidates.reported_accuracy: Self-reported (Speechmatics, Mar 6 2026): Arabic–English code-switching WER 6.3% vs Google 9.7% ('35% lower'), Arabic-only WER 4.5% vs Google 5.9%. The benchmark set is not identified. No independent Egyptian code-switching number was found; Speechmatics was not in the Perle benchmark.

Pricing FAQ: 'If you have not opted in to the model training discount programme, Realtime audio is never stored, and Batch data auto-deletes after 7 days or sooner via the API, and your data is never used to improve our models.' Accuracy claims are vendor-reported only, so it is worth an A/B test against ElevenLabs on the user's own calls. SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and GDPR certified.

candidates.name: Google Gemini 3.5 Transcribe (Gemini API / Google AI Studio)
candidates.cost_and_free_tier: Free tier: input and output are 'Free of charge'. Paid: $2.00 per 1M audio tokens (≈$0.003/min) input and $12.00 per 1M text tokens (≈$0.002/min) output, 'effective blended rate of ~$0.005 per min'. Free-tier rate limits are only shown in AI Studio; the docs publish no numbers. Needs a Google account and API key, no card. Egypt and Saudi Arabia are listed available regions. Released 26 Aug 2026; model page last updated August 2026.
candidates.egyptian_arabic: 'Arabic (Egypt) ar-EG' is explicitly listed. It is the only Arabic locale on the model page.
candidates.code_switching: Official: 'handles multi-language code-switching'; 'Handles intra-sentence and inter-sentential code-switching without manual configuration'; 'Includes mid-session code-mixing.' Output script for English words in Arabic speech is not documented.
candidates.diarization: mode.diarization_mode='speaker' returns spk_1, spk_2 labels. Up to 8 speakers; 'Attribution for 3+ speakers is experimental'. Diarization is incompatible with custom vocabulary. The launch blog says 'up to three speakers'.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Hosted. Limits: 'Up to 1 hour per request (up to 30 minutes when speaker diarization or word-level timestamps are enabled)'. Upload via the Files API: 2 GB per file, 20 GB per project, files stored 48 h, free. The user's 16–80 min calls therefore need chunks of 30 min or less when diarizing. Speaker IDs are not guaranteed consistent across chunks, so re-link them locally (e.g., the user's WeSpeaker embeddings).
candidates.reported_accuracy: Self-reported: average WER 2.6% non-streaming and 4.0% streaming 'as measured by Artificial Analysis'; FLEURS WER 5.04% batch and 5.50% streaming. No Arabic or Egyptian code-switching numbers were published. No independent Egyptian code-switching benchmark was found.

The pricing page says 'Used to improve our products: Yes' for the free tier and 'No' for paid. The terms add that for unpaid services 'human reviewers may read, annotate, and process your API input and output' and 'Do not submit sensitive, confidential, or personal information.' On paid, prompts are logged only for abuse detection for a limited period. Free is not allowed for EEA, UK or Swiss users. Must be 18+.

candidates.name: pyannote speaker-diarization-community-1 (pyannote.audio 4.0.x)
candidates.license: Weights CC-BY-4.0. pyannote.audio code MIT. Embedding sub-model is WeSpeaker ResNet34-LM, VoxCeleb-derived, also CC-BY-4.0.
candidates.cost_and_free_tier: Free to run locally. The HF repo is gated: you need a free HF account, must accept the conditions (share contact info) and use a read token for the first download. After that it can run offline. There is an ungated mirror at pyannote-community/speaker-diarization-community-1, but it is run by an unverified 'Unofficial Pyannote Community' org with 1 member, so use it at your own risk. pyannoteAI also hosts community-1 at EUR 0.035/h.
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Weights are about 33.7 MB total (segmentation 5.9 MB, embedding 26.6 MB, PLDA 0.26 MB). Needs PyTorch: pyannote.audio 4.0.7 requires torch>=2.8, torchaudio, torchcodec (FFmpeg), lightning and opentelemetry. On Linux the default PyPI torch wheel is 555 MB plus CUDA deps (for example nvidia-cudnn-cu13 is 519 MB). The CPU-only wheel from download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu is about 184 MB, so install from that index. There is no official CPU speed figure; the only official speed is 31 s per hour of audio on an H100. Community CPU reports vary widely: RTF 0.5-1 in older threads, 3.1 runs more than 2x slower than 3.0 on CPU, and one 2026 paper measured a pyannote-3.1-based pipeline on Apple M4 CPU at RTF 1.84 with a 1 s segmentation stride vs 0.22 with a 3 s stride. So for 16-80 min calls on an i5-1245U expect anywhere from about 0.2x to more than 1x real time. Unverified; measure it. To speed it up, the maintainer suggests increasing the segmentation step.
candidates.diarization: Pipeline: powerset segmentation (up to 3 local speakers per 10 s chunk, overlap-aware), then WeSpeaker ResNet34-LM embeddings (embedding_exclude_overlap: true), then PLDA and VBx clustering (threshold 0.6, Fa 0.07, Fb 0.8). Supports num_speakers, min_speakers and max_speakers. New in 4.0: output.exclusive_speaker_diarization, which keeps only one speaker active at a time and is meant for aligning STT word timestamps. Audio is downmixed to mono and resampled to 16 kHz automatically, so 8 kHz WAV is accepted. Telemetry is ON by default and sends pipeline origin, file duration and num/min/max_speakers to otel.pyannote.ai. Disable it with PYANNOTE_METRICS_ENABLED=0 or set_telemetry_metrics(False, save_choice_as_default=True).
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Diarization works on acoustics and is language-agnostic. The segmentation training data (AISHELL, AliMeeting, AMI, AVA-AVD, DIHARD, Ego4D, MSDWild, REPERE, VoxConverse) contains no telephone/CALLHOME data. One secondary benchmark (Soniqo, 0.25 s collar, no speaker count given) reports community-1 at 15.57% DER on an internal Arabic set, the best of the systems listed there. That set's dialect and channel are not disclosed.
candidates.code_switching: Not relevant to diarization. Speaker assignment ignores which language is spoken.
candidates.reported_accuracy: Official, self-reported (no collar, overlap scored, no oracle speaker count, no tuning). CALLHOME part 2: 3.1 = 28.5, community-1 = 26.7, precision-2 = 16.6. AMI IHM 17.0, DIHARD3 20.2, VoxConverse 11.2, AISHELL-4 11.7, AliMeeting 20.3. CALLHOME is its worst dataset (out of domain: telephone, 8 kHz). These numbers are NOT comparable to NVIDIA/ETH numbers, which use a 0.25 s collar.
candidates.notes: Best first try for local use. It uses the same WeSpeaker ResNet34 embedding you already use, but adds neural overlap-aware segmentation, PLDA+VBx clustering and an exclusive-mode output. Recipe: pipeline(audio, num_speakers=2), then take output.exclusive_speaker_diarization. Run faster-whisper large-v3 with word_timestamps=True. Give each word the speaker whose exclusive segment contains the word's midpoint (fall back to the nearest segment), then merge consecutive same-speaker words into turns. Set PYANNOTE_METRICS_ENABLED=0 so no metadata leaves the machine. The community-1 config uses segmentation_batch_size and embedding_batch_size of 32; lower them if RAM is tight.

For code-switched text, faster-whisper's own word_timestamps are the safer source of word times.

candidates.name: Best practice: combining diarization with Whisper word timestamps (exclusive mode + midpoint/overlap assignment + smoothing)
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Negligible cost.
candidates.diarization: 1) Use a non-overlapping speaker timeline. pyannote exclusive mode: 'only one speaker (the most likely to be transcribed) is active at any given time, dramatically simplifying the alignment between STT word timestamps and speaker labels'. 2) Get word times from faster-whisper (word_timestamps=True). 3) Assign each word to the speaker active at its midpoint (NVIDIA's Nemotron blog) or with maximum overlap, falling back to the nearest segment (WhisperX assign_word_speakers with fill_nearest). 4) Smooth the result: merge consecutive same-speaker words into turns, and optionally snap turn changes to sentence punctuation (the whisper-diarization realignment idea). 5) Optional: LLM post-correction à la DiarizationLM (fine-tuned PaLM 2-S cut WDER by 55.5% relative on Fisher and 44.9% on CALLHOME English; the open implementation is a best-effort replica and English-centric).
candidates.egyptian_arabic: Whisper's DTW word timestamps do not depend on a character dictionary, so they work for mixed Arabic/Latin output. WhisperX's Arabic wav2vec2 aligner does not handle Latin script (wildcard mapping, then interpolation).
candidates.code_switching: Use faster-whisper's own word timestamps, or ctc-forced-aligner with --romanize, rather than a language-specific wav2vec2 aligner.
candidates.reported_accuracy: DiarizationLM: see above. Other steps are unquantified.
candidates.notes: Short Egyptian backchannels ('aywa', 'tamam', 'ah') are where word-level speaker errors concentrate. Exclusive mode plus the midpoint rule handles most of them.

candidates.name: Best practice: 8 kHz telephone audio (bandwidth, embedding choice, channels, install hygiene)
candidates.cpu_feasibility: Install the CPU-only PyTorch wheel (about 184 MB from download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu). The default PyPI Linux torch is 555 MB plus multi-GB CUDA deps, which is painful at 1.5 MB/s.
candidates.diarization: (a) Almost every model expects 16 kHz: pyannote resamples automatically; sherpa-onnx CLI, Falcon, Senko and Sortformer/Nemotron need 16 kHz input. Upsampling adds no information, so the real fix is embeddings trained on telephone data: VBx ResNet101_8kHz (SRE Mixer + Switchboard), TitaNet (Fisher/Switchboard/SRE), and Sortformer/Nemotron (Fisher and CALLHOME part 1 in training). WeSpeaker VoxCeleb ResNet34, used by pyannote and by you now, is trained only on wideband data. (b) If the call recorder can save stereo (one party per channel), channel-based diarization is exact (ElevenLabs use_multi_channel, Speechmatics channel diarization). Azure diarization is mono only. (c) Keep an overlap-aware segmenter (pyannote powerset or Sortformer) but score and assign words in exclusive mode. (d) For more than 30 min with VBx AHC, use random initialization. (e) Disable pyannote telemetry (PYANNOTE_METRICS_ENABLED=0). (f) Measure DER on 2-3 of your own calls you label by hand, using dscore or pyannote.metrics with a 0.25 s collar, rather than trusting cross-paper numbers. Collar and oracle settings differ between sources: pyannote uses no collar; NVIDIA, ETH, VBx 'Fair' and Soniqo use 0.25 s.
candidates.egyptian_arabic: LDC CALLHOME Egyptian Arabic is 8 kHz Cairene telephone speech, and the NIST 2000 CALLHOME diarization set includes Arabic. Whether that Arabic is the Egyptian CallHome data is not confirmed.

candidates.notes: Suggested local order to try on your laptop: (1) pyannote community-1 with num_speakers=2, exclusive mode and CPU torch. (2) sherpa-onnx with segmentation-3.0 int8, TitaNet-L and num_clusters=2 as the fast torch-free fallback. (3) Nemotron-3-Diarization q8 via NeMo-Speech.cpp CPU as the telephone-trained contender (brand new). (4) DiariZen base in a separate venv if accuracy is still lacking. Merge each with faster-whisper large-v3 words. This ordering is my synthesis, not a published result.
